title: Old Souqs: Markets of the Past
summary: How the old covered souqs of historic Arab and Islamic cities were organized by craft, why they became the social and economic heart of the city, and how they differ from a modern mall.
poll: An old souq is a better place to shop than a modern mall.

versions.title: Old Souqs
versions.text:
A souq is an old kind of market. It is in the old part of many Arab cities. It is often near the main mosque.

A souq is not one big room. It is many thin lanes side by side. A roof of wood or cloth gives shade. The hot sun cannot get in.

Each part of the souq sells one kind of thing. One lane has spice. One lane has gold. One lane has cloth. One lane has pots made of metal.

One family may run the same stall for many years. A boy can learn the trade from his dad.

At a souq, you do not pay the first price. You talk with the seller. This is a bargain. Both sides like to talk and smile.

The souq is not just for shopping. Friends meet there. People share news. They sit and drink tea at a small stall.

A new mall is one big building with cool air. A souq is old lanes full of shade and sun.

Some souqs are still open today. You can go see them and shop too.

Many visitors paused to rest and partake of tea or coffee at a diminutive stall tucked between the larger shops, transforming a simple errand into a genuine social occasion capable of stretching across an entire afternoon without anyone remarking upon the passage of time.

A modern shopping mall, by comparison, constitutes a single large building saturated with machine-generated air and fixed price tags affixed to every shelf, where a customer rarely exchanges more than a cursory word with a clerk before proceeding to the next establishment. A souq, by stark contrast, remains an enduring labyrinth of ancient lanes suffused with shade, clamor, rich aromas, and sunlight filtering through gaps in the overhead roof, a living remnant of how commerce once functioned throughout the entire region long before large enclosed buildings supplanted these open lanes.

Many souqs remain open today across the region, meticulously preserved as integral components of each city's cultural heritage. Visitors can wander the narrow lanes, observe craftsmen at their trade, and purchase spice, cloth, or gold precisely as customers did countless generations before them, perpetuating a custom that has outlasted innumerable transformations to the city that grew up around it across the centuries.

HIGH.modelAnswer: The souq's narrow, shaded lanes supported commerce because sellers of the same craft clustered together, which let customers easily compare quality and bargain over price for spice, cloth, or metal goods. The same covered lanes also supported the souq's social role, since the shade encouraged people to linger, meet friends, and share news rather than hurry through, turning errands into lasting social occasions. Because apprentices learned crafts from their fathers within these same lanes, each generation renewed both the commerce and the heritage of the souq at once, something a modern mall's single climate-controlled building rarely replicates.
